warning-potterycrafts-sds-p3303-h302-har: Warning (Potterycrafts SDS P3303): H302 harmful if swallowed; do not ingest and avoid breathing the dust.
tricalcium-phosphate-real-bone-ash-may-u: Tricalcium phosphate. Real bone ash may contain a little CaCO₃ and so a small LOI.
warning-potterycrafts-sds-h302-harmful-i: Warning (Potterycrafts SDS): H302 harmful if swallowed; H315 causes skin irritation; H319 causes serious eye irritation; H335 dry dust may cause respiratory irritation.
danger-eu-classification-nexchem-sds-h36: Danger (EU classification, Nexchem SDS): H360FD may damage fertility or the unborn child; H319 causes serious eye irritation; avoid breathing the dust. (Etimine USA''s US sheet: Warning H303/H319/H361d.)
Danger (EU classification, Nexchem SDS): H360FD may damage fertility or the unborn child; avoid breathing the dust. (Etimine USA''s US sheet: Warning H303/H361d.)
the-ideal-mineral-2cao-3b2o3-5h2o-plfjql: The ideal mineral, 2CaO•3B₂O₃•5H₂O, with 50.8% B₂O₃. Real colemanite has less boron, about 40%: see Colemanite (commercial). Not the same as the calcium borate frit in UK recipes.
not-classified-etimine-sds-may-irritate-: Not classified (Etimine SDS); may irritate the eyes; avoid breathing the dust.
turkish-colemanite-etimine-s-typical-ana: Turkish colemanite, Etimine’s typical analysis (standard and fine mesh). Scarce in US retail; Gerstley Borate and Gillespie Borate are the usual stand-ins.
not-classified-etimine-sds-the-natural-2: Not classified (Etimine SDS); the natural ore contains 8–12% calcite and 6–8% clay, and CTM''s SDS notes traces of arsenic sulphides; avoid breathing the dust.
theoretical-kaolin-the-ideal-formula-of-: Theoretical kaolin, the ideal formula of clay. Real kaolins run 12–13.5% LOI and carry some iron, titania and alkali.
not-classified-ctm-sds-45-104-to3q1: Not classified (CTM SDS 45/104); less than 1% respirable quartz; avoid breathing the dust.
danger-fluorsid-synthetic-cryolite-sds-h: Danger (Fluorsid synthetic cryolite SDS): H332 harmful if inhaled; H362 may harm breast-fed children; H372 damages lungs and bones (skeletal fluorosis) through repeated exposure; H411 toxic to aquatic life; releases fluorine in firing, so ventilate the kiln.
not-classified-potterycrafts-sds-breathi: Not classified (Potterycrafts SDS); breathing the dust over long periods raises the risk of lung disease.
typical-formula-not-quarried-since-2006-: Typical formula. Not quarried since 2006; what is sold now are synthetic substitutes with different chemistry, so use the supplier’s analysis for those.
fine-dust-contains-respirable-crystallin: Fine dust contains respirable crystalline silica; avoid breathing it.
an-old-north-american-potash-feldspar-er: An old North American potash feldspar, high in silica, found only in US references; a Glazy recipe taken from Grebanier''s Chinese Stoneware Glazes calls for ''Godfrey or Maine feldspar''. Listed as no longer available by 1999 (Zamek, Ceramics Monthly). No supplier sells it now.
typical-formula-higher-ratio-of-fluxes-u: Typical formula. Higher ratio of fluxes makes this material melt at lower temps than most feldspars.
not-classified-sibelco-sds-gb-ie-39by50: Not classified (Sibelco SDS, GB/IE); avoid breathing the dust.
warning-ctm-potash-feldspar-sds-49-55a3f: Warning (CTM potash feldspar SDS 49): H373 may damage the lungs through repeated inhalation, as it contains 5–10% fine crystalline silica; avoid breathing the dust.
an-old-us-potash-feldspar-that-1xt7e2g: An old US potash feldspar that has been unavailable since at least the 1990s. NM Clay names G-200 EU as a substitute for Oxford; a current potash feldspar plus a little silica comes closest, since Oxford is lower in alkali and higher in silica.
contains-crystalline-silica-avoid-breath: Contains crystalline silica; avoid breathing the dust.
danger-ctm-sds-51-h372-causes-hrnahm: Danger (CTM SDS 51): H372 causes damage to organs through repeated inhalation; 25–50% fine crystalline silica; avoid breathing the dust.
warning-seaforth-mineral-ore-sds-acid-1e: Warning (Seaforth Mineral & Ore SDS, acid grade): may be harmful if swallowed or inhaled and may irritate skin, eyes and airways; 0.09–2.8% crystalline silica; releases fluorine in firing.
warning-ctm-sds-24-h302-harmful-s4gzl: Warning (CTM SDS 24): H302 harmful if swallowed; H319 causes serious eye irritation.
mgco3-the-mineral-magnesite-slightly-sol: MgCO₃, the mineral magnesite. Slightly soluble. Potters usually buy light magnesium carbonate, which has less MgO: see Light Magnesium Carbonate.
not-classified-ctm-sds-58-less-eqn4tu: Not classified (CTM SDS 58); less than 1% quartz; avoid breathing the dust.
hydromagnesite-the-light-fluffy-magnesiu: Hydromagnesite, the light, fluffy magnesium carbonate potters usually buy: 43.1% MgO, less than magnesite. Slightly soluble.
not-classified-ctm-magnesium-carbonate-s: Not classified (CTM magnesium carbonate SDS 58); avoid breathing the dust.
warning-fisher-uk-sds-potassium-nitrate-: Warning (Fisher UK SDS, potassium nitrate): H272 may intensify fire (oxidiser); keep away from combustibles.
warning-fisher-uk-sds-potassium-carbonat: Warning (Fisher UK SDS, potassium carbonate): H315 causes skin irritation; H319 causes serious eye irritation; H335 may cause respiratory irritation.
dust-hazard-from-free-silica-particles-f: Dust hazard from free silica particles.
danger-ctm-silica-flour-sds-53-1tgs6do: Danger (CTM silica flour SDS 53): H372 damages the lungs through repeated inhalation; over 10% respirable quartz; avoid breathing the dust.
warning-ctm-sds-69-h319-causes-61w3d2: Warning (CTM SDS 69): H319 causes serious eye irritation.
warning-fisher-uk-sds-h272-may-1oy6zbu: Warning (Fisher UK SDS): H272 may intensify fire (oxidiser); H319 causes serious eye irritation.
the-ideal-mineral-li2o-al2o3-4sio2-1n0rm: The ideal mineral, Li₂O•Al₂O₃•4SiO₂, with 8.0% Li₂O. Commercial grades carry less lithium, about 7.1–7.65% Li₂O, with some iron, potash and phosphorus; use the supplier’s analysis when you have it.
not-classified-potterycrafts-sds-p3357-c: Not classified (Potterycrafts SDS P3357); contains 4–6% quartz; avoid breathing the dust.
not-classified-ctm-sds-40-the-xaqm6l: Not classified (CTM SDS 40); the powder may irritate eyes and skin; avoid breathing the dust.
not-classified-ctm-sds-54-ctm-3ezprp: Not classified (CTM SDS 54; CTM''s pottery talc is about 55–60% talc and 40–45% magnesium carbonate, under 1% quartz); avoid breathing the dust.
not-classified-under-eu-rules-kronos-6o0: Not classified under EU rules (KRONOS SDS, non-pigmentary grade; CTM SDS 26 agrees); avoid breathing the dust.
not-classified-ctm-sds-55-may-al0thq: Not classified (CTM SDS 55); may contain some crystalline silica; avoid breathing the dust.
toxic-will-volatilize-at-1742-f-1ger4wq: Toxic. Will volatilize at 1742 F (950 C) in reduction.
warning-ctm-sds-27-h400-h410-1ie0hx7: Warning (CTM SDS 27): H400/H410 very toxic to aquatic life with long-lasting effects; do not wash into drains.
for-decades-the-most-common-us-1xxnyd4: For decades the most common US potash feldspar, mined in South Dakota until Pacer shut down in 2023. Use G-200 EU or Mahavir instead; they are lower in iron, but test, because the swap is not always 1:1.
toxic-chromium-is-counted-as-cr2o3-1v1l4: Toxic. Chromium is counted as Cr₂O₃; the LOI is the oxygen released as it decomposes.
danger-fisher-uk-sds-h272-oxidiser-13f3s: Danger (Fisher UK SDS): H272 oxidiser; H301 toxic if swallowed; H312 harmful in contact with skin; H330 fatal if inhaled; H314 causes severe burns; H317/H334 skin and respiratory sensitiser; H340 may cause genetic defects; H350 may cause cancer; H360FD may damage fertility or the unborn child; H372 causes organ damage; H410 very toxic to aquatic life.
toxic-heavy-metal-serious-hazard-from-jf: Toxic heavy metal. Serious hazard from dust, can leach into solutions. Trace amounts can cause behavior changes in children and hamper learning.
danger-fisher-uk-sds-pb3o4-h302-2544rq: Danger (Fisher UK SDS, Pb3O4): H302+H332 harmful if swallowed or inhaled; H351 suspected of causing cancer; H360Df may damage the unborn child; H362 may harm breast-fed children; H372 causes organ damage through repeated exposure; H410 very toxic to aquatic life.
danger-fisher-uk-sds-basic-lead-io9skd: Danger (Fisher UK SDS, basic lead carbonate): H302+H332 harmful if swallowed or inhaled; H360Df may damage the unborn child, suspected of damaging fertility; H373 may cause organ damage through repeated exposure; H410 very toxic to aquatic life.
danger-carl-roth-sds-lead-ii-gu86j: Danger (Carl Roth SDS, lead(II) oxide): H302+H332 harmful if swallowed or inhaled; H351 suspected of causing cancer; H360Df may damage the unborn child; H362 may harm breast-fed children; H372 damages kidneys, nervous system and blood-forming system; H410 very toxic to aquatic life.
potash-feldspar-from-spain-made-by-1192t: Potash feldspar from Spain, made by flotation from feldspathic sand and imported by Imerys as the replacement for G-200 after the Georgia mine closed. The data sheet gives 70% K-feldspar, 23% Na-feldspar and 7% quartz.
contains-crystalline-silica-quartz-about: Contains crystalline silica (quartz, about 7%); avoid breathing the dust.
white-firing-indian-potash-feldspar-that: White-firing Indian potash feldspar that Laguna imports as the successor to G-200, and the potash feldspar named on Glazy''s shopping list. It has slightly more K2O and SiO2 and slightly less Al2O3 than the old G-200.
contains-crystalline-silica-free-quartz-: Contains crystalline silica (free quartz 10-15% per the data sheet); avoid breathing the dust.
200-mesh-flotation-grade-soda-feldspar-n: 200-mesh flotation-grade soda feldspar from Spruce Pine, NC, formerly called NC-4. It is the standard US replacement for Kona F-4.
contains-crystalline-silica-about-10-qua: Contains crystalline silica (about 10% quartz per the SDS); avoid breathing the dust.
silica-deficient-sodium-potassium-alumin: Silica-deficient sodium-potassium aluminosilicate (albite, microcline and nepheline) from Ontario, a stronger flux than soda feldspar. A-270 is the usual pottery grade; A-200 and A-400 have the same chemistry and differ only in particle size (A-400 is finer).
covia-states-there-is-no-free-1893lq7: Covia states there is no free crystalline silica (<0.1%), but avoid breathing the dust.
spodumene-concentrate-sold-by-laguna-the: Spodumene concentrate sold by Laguna, the spodumene most US pottery retailers stock (Clay-Planet and Marjon list the Laguna product). It is a lithium source that melts more readily than lithium carbonate and lowers glaze expansion.
contains-crystalline-silica-5-40-quartz-: Contains crystalline silica (5-40% quartz per Laguna''s SDS); avoid breathing the dust. Some spodumene causes bubbles in the glaze slurry.
lithium-aluminosilicate-with-very-low-th: Lithium aluminosilicate with very low thermal expansion, used to fight crazing and thermal shock. It does not cause the slurry frothing that some spodumene does.
natural-calcium-silicate-the-wollastonit: Natural calcium silicate, the wollastonite most US pottery suppliers sell (Laguna, Seattle Pottery Supply and Bailey stock Vansil grades). It supplies CaO and SiO2 together with no carbonate gas, so it causes less pinholing than whiting.
needle-shaped-acicular-mineral-dust-avoi: Needle-shaped (acicular) mineral dust; avoid breathing it.
high-purity-new-york-wollastonite-with-1: High-purity New York wollastonite with low LOI. Imerys markets NYAD M200, M325 and M400 grades for ceramic bodies and glazes; Sheffield Pottery sells NYAD-G.
a-cornwall-stone-replacement-from-hammil: A Cornwall stone replacement from Hammill & Gillespie, with a typical makeup of about 20% quartz, 52% albite and 27% orthoclase. Unlike the real Cornish stone, which has not been quarried since 2006, it contains no fluorine.
contains-crystalline-silica-about-20-qua: Contains crystalline silica (about 20% quartz); avoid breathing the dust.
laguna-s-blended-cornwall-stone-substitu: Laguna''s blended Cornwall stone substitute (feldspar, quartz and a little kaolin), developed when natural Cornish stone became unavailable. It is nearly iron-free.
contains-crystalline-silica-10-25-quartz: Contains crystalline silica (10-25% quartz per Laguna''s 2024 SDS); avoid breathing the dust.
indian-potash-feldspar-from-imerys-impor: Indian potash feldspar from Imerys, imported by Hammill & Gillespie since about 2024 as another G-200 and Custer replacement. Its chemistry is close to G-200 EU.
the-standard-us-potash-feldspar-for-saiz: The standard US potash feldspar for decades, blended at Monticello, Georgia, from about 70% high-potash G-200 HP and 30% Minspar 200 soda feldspar. Use G-200 EU or Mahavir for old recipes.
high-potash-feldspar-that-laguna-sold-1a: High-potash feldspar that Laguna sold as ''G-200 New Potash'' after the original G-200 blend ended. Laguna also sold a 3:7 Minspar 200 : G-200 HP mix as ''G200 Old Blend'' to match the old chemistry.
a-popular-north-american-soda-feldspar-1: A popular North American soda feldspar that is no longer made; Minspar 200 has very similar chemistry and is the usual replacement.
a-fluorine-bearing-lithium-potassium-mic: A fluorine-bearing lithium-potassium mica, long unavailable to US potters. There is no direct replacement; supply the Li2O from spodumene, petalite or lithium carbonate, and the K2O from a potash feldspar.
jeff-zamek-s-1997-guide-to-plkif7: Jeff Zamek''s 1997 guide to substitutions in Ceramics Monthly already called it discontinued.
contains-fluorine-which-is-released-as-1: Contains fluorine, which is released as fumes during firing and can cause glaze bubbles and pitting; ventilate the kiln.
a-water-washed-secondary-kaolin-from-1i5: A water-washed secondary kaolin from Edgar, Florida, long the standard US glaze kaolin because it suspends glazes well and fires white. Supply stopped around 2023 to 2025 and US suppliers now recommend Wilco UPF Georgia kaolin in its place.
contains-crystalline-silica-quartz-do-no: Contains crystalline silica (quartz); do not breathe the dust.
a-white-firing-georgia-kaolin-that-1k8rp: A white-firing Georgia kaolin that US suppliers now stock in place of EPK. Potters report one-for-one swaps for EPK in cone 6 and cone 10 glazes with little visible change, though it carries more TiO2 (1.5%) than EPK (0.4%).
an-air-floated-georgia-kaolin-and-1f3wll: An air-floated Georgia kaolin and the most plastic kaolin commonly sold in North America. It helps suspend glazes but is not thixotropic like EPK, and its TiO2 (1.4%) makes it fire less white than EPK.
a-fine-plastic-kentucky-ball-clay-1l3mfw: A fine, plastic Kentucky ball clay, the usual US ''ball clay'' in glaze and body recipes. In glazes it adds alumina and silica and helps keep the slurry suspended; it fires off-white to buff because of its iron and titanium.
a-325-mesh-calcined-kaolin-made-843pbe: A 325-mesh calcined kaolin made for paints and sold by US pottery suppliers as their calcined kaolin. Use it in place of part of the raw kaolin in high-clay glazes to cut drying shrinkage and crawling.
kaolin-fired-to-drive-off-its-47owxv: Kaolin fired to drive off its chemical water, with the same chemistry as kaolin minus the LOI. Recipes listing plain ''calcined kaolin'' can use this.
a-red-burning-iron-rich-ohio-91msbo: A red-burning, iron-rich Ohio earthenware clay, air-floated to 200 mesh. In glazes it is a source of iron (about 7% Fe2O3) and alkali, used up to 60% in some brown and slip-type glazes.
a-plastic-cream-burning-southern-ohio-d7: A plastic, cream-burning southern Ohio stoneware clay, air-floated to 200 mesh. Mostly a body clay; in glazes it supplies alumina and silica with some iron and titanium.
contains-crystalline-silica-quartz-do-no: Contains crystalline silica (quartz); do not breathe the dust. Contains some sulfur.
a-plastic-buff-firing-missouri-fireclay-: A plastic, buff-firing Missouri fireclay sold in 20, 35, 40 and 50 mesh grinds. Mostly a body clay; the values are typical for a natural clay.
a-blended-iron-bearing-slip-clay-1wfl7qj: A blended iron-bearing slip clay that Plainsman has made since 1988 as a substitute for Albany slip. On its own it melts to a glossy brown at cone 10 (tenmoku in reduction) and needs about 20% frit at cone 6; use a roasted and raw mix in high-percentage recipes to avoid drying cracks.
a-silty-iron-rich-new-york-oucatm: A silty, iron-rich New York clay that melted by itself into a glossy dark brown glaze at cone 8 to 10 and appears in thousands of older recipes. It has been out of production since the late 1980s; use Alberta Slip in its place.
leadless-low-alumina-calcium-sodium-boro: Leadless, low-alumina calcium-sodium borosilicate frit; the most-used frit in North American glaze recipes, mainly as a boron and calcium source. Fusion 1450 F, flow 1600 F, CTE 9.47 (Ferro 2008).
non-hazardous-glass-powder-per-supplier-: Non-hazardous glass powder per supplier SDS; avoid breathing dust.
calcium-borosilicate-frit-with-a-balance: Calcium borosilicate frit with a balanced, glaze-like chemistry (contains about 10% alumina); with a little kaolin it is nearly a complete low-fire glaze. Fusion 1600 F, flow 1750 F, CTE 7.94 (Ferro 2008).
high-sodium-low-boron-high-expansion-ggm: High-sodium, low-boron, high-expansion frit; a common soda source at all temperatures and in crystalline glazes. Fusion 1400 F, flow 1700 F, CTE 10.08 (Ferro 2008).
well-balanced-high-boron-calcium-borosil: Well-balanced high-boron calcium borosilicate frit; about 85 frit to 15 kaolin makes a clear cone 04 glaze. Fusion 1500 F, flow 1700 F, CTE 7.16 (Ferro 2008).
alkali-free-magnesia-borosilicate-frit-w: Alkali-free magnesia borosilicate frit with very low thermal expansion (CTE about 4.0); used at 3-10% to cure crazing and as a low-melting MgO source. Fusion 1900 F, flow 2300 F (Ferro 2003).
high-alkali-almost-calcium-free-alkali-3: High-alkali, almost calcium-free alkali borosilicate frit with a little zinc and fluorine; high expansion, used for crackle and alkaline-color glazes. Fusion 1400 F, flow 1500 F, CTE 9.98 (Ferro 2008).
contains-about-1-5-fluorine-which-q7b1ho: Contains about 1.5% fluorine, which can be released during firing; ventilate the kiln. Otherwise a low-hazard glass powder.
artware-flux-calcium-borosilicate-frit-f: Artware flux calcium borosilicate frit; Fusion''s listed equivalent of Vibrantz 3134. Versus 3134-2 (Ferro 2008): Al2O3 -1.20, B2O3 +1.01, SiO2 -0.56, CaO +0.49, Na2O +0.26 points; it melts slightly more fluidly.
boro-calcium-dinnerware-frit-fusion-s-lb: Boro-calcium dinnerware frit; Fusion''s listed equivalent of Vibrantz 3124. Versus 3124-2 (Ferro 2008): B2O3 +0.86, K2O -0.68 (none in F-19), Na2O +0.60, SiO2 -0.44, Al2O3 -0.31 points; it flows a little more.
high-calcium-boron-leadless-frit-fusion-: High-calcium boron leadless frit; Fusion''s listed equivalent of Vibrantz 3195. It is the least exact of these matches: versus 3195-2 (Ferro 2008) it has K2O +3.70, Na2O -2.69, B2O3 -2.32, Al2O3 +1.52, CaO -0.86, SiO2 +0.65 points.
high-sodium-low-boron-frit-fusion-16l28b: High-sodium, low-boron frit; Fusion''s listed equivalent of Vibrantz 3110 and the closest of these matches: every oxide is within 0.26 points of 3110-2 (Ferro 2008). It flows slightly more and has lower surface tension.
alkali-free-magnesia-borosilicate-frit-w: Alkali-free magnesia borosilicate frit with very low expansion (CTE 3.96), used against crazing; Fusion''s listed equivalent of Vibrantz 3249. Versus 3249 it has no CaO (-3.50 points), SiO2 +2.40, B2O3 +1.30, Al2O3 -0.80, MgO +0.60.
natural-sodium-calcium-borate-ore-colema: Natural sodium-calcium borate ore (colemanite and ulexite with a hectorite-like clay), long the main low- and mid-fire boron flux in US recipes. The mine closed in 2000; remaining stock is limited and costly, and Gillespie Borate is the recommended pound-for-pound replacement.
borate-do-not-ingest-high-dose-kpnwt9: Borate: do not ingest; high-dose animal studies of inorganic borates show reproductive/developmental effects (U.S. Borax Gerstley Borate MSDS, Apr 2013). Avoid breathing dust. Supplier carries a California Prop 65 crystalline-silica warning.
blended-borate-mainly-ulexite-with-some-: Blended borate (mainly ulexite with some colemanite and about 10% clay-like material) made as a pound-for-pound replacement for Gerstley Borate; currently produced and sold in the US, UK and Europe.
borate-do-not-ingest-high-dose-havqf3: Borate: do not ingest; high-dose animal studies of inorganic borates show reproductive/developmental effects (U.S. Borax Gerstley Borate MSDS, Apr 2013). Avoid breathing dust.
legacy-blended-gerstley-borate-substitut: Legacy blended Gerstley Borate substitute sold by Laguna in the 2000s; keep only for old recipes. It needed 6-8 parts bentonite or hectorite per 100 to match Gerstley Borate''s suspension; Gillespie Borate is the current replacement.
laguna-withdrew-it-in-2012-its-13jz0u3: Laguna withdrew it in 2012: its safety sheet was replaced that May by a note that, with plentiful Gerstley Borate again, Laguna Borate was no longer available.
borate-do-not-ingest-high-dose-13mdgfk: Borate: do not ingest; high-dose animal studies of inorganic borates show reproductive/developmental effects (U.S. Borax Gerstley Borate MSDS, Apr 2013). Avoid breathing dust. Laguna''s MSDS lists crystalline silica and calcium carbonate.
legacy-plastic-gerstley-borate-substitut: Legacy plastic Gerstley Borate substitute developed by Plainsman Clays in 2000 and sold in the early 2000s; no longer made. Keep only for old recipes; Gillespie Borate is the current replacement.
plainsman-s-materials-page-listed-it-388: Plainsman''s materials page listed it until late 2017 and no longer did in January 2018.
commercial-turkish-sodium-calcium-borate: Commercial Turkish sodium-calcium borate ore, sold ground (75 and 45 micron grades); a raw boron source used mainly by European and Russian potters and in home-made Gerstley Borate substitutes. It is slightly soluble and loses about a third of its weight on firing.
borate-do-not-ingest-high-dose-1q1jdvy: Borate: do not ingest; high-dose animal studies of inorganic borates show reproductive/developmental effects (U.S. Borax Gerstley Borate MSDS, Apr 2013). Avoid breathing dust. Etimine''s SDS (rev. Oct 2021) lists it as not classified under UN GHS.
aluminum-hydroxide-powder-used-to-add-8q: Aluminum hydroxide powder used to add alumina to glazes and in kiln wash and wadding; it suspends and adheres better than calcined alumina. It loses about 35% of its weight as water near 220-300 C.
calcined-aluminum-oxide-ground-to-325-43: Calcined aluminum oxide ground to -325 mesh; very refractory (melts about 2040 C), used for matting and stiffening glazes and in kiln wash. Only very fine grades dissolve fully in a glaze.
low-hazard-nuisance-dust-avoid-breathing: Low hazard nuisance dust; avoid breathing it.
blended-cornish-china-clay-from-imerys-6: Blended Cornish china clay from Imerys with very little titania and about 2% K2O, so it fires blue-white. It is the usual kaolin in UK porcelain bodies and many UK glaze recipes.
fine-dust-may-contain-traces-of-1caabb5: Fine dust; may contain traces of crystalline silica.
imerys-cornish-china-clay-with-more-1xib: Imerys Cornish china clay with more plasticity and slightly less iron and potash than Grolleg; very white firing. Made for porcelain bodies and used in glazes like any kaolin.
imerys-calcined-cornish-china-clay-about: Imerys calcined Cornish china clay (about 55% mullite, 45% glass). Fine grades replace part of the raw clay in high-clay glazes to cut shrinkage and crawling, and raise the maturing temperature slightly.
high-silica-devon-ball-clay-with-all38y: High-silica Devon ball clay with good plasticity, medium strength and low iron; fires ivory buff. A common ball clay in UK glazes and slips.
dorset-ball-clay-with-high-strength-cu8i: Dorset ball clay with high strength and fairly high iron (about 2.3% Fe2O3), used in warm-coloured stoneware bodies and in some UK glazes and slips.
low-plasticity-white-firing-ball-clay-2z: Low-plasticity, white-firing ball clay sold by Potclays, popular in stoneware bodies; whiter firing than TWVA.
blend-of-medium-plasticity-white-firing-: Blend of medium-plasticity white-firing ball clays. Potclays sells it as the replacement for ESVA ball clay, which the producers phased out.
potclays-potash-feldspar-almost-no-soda-: Potclays'' potash feldspar: almost no soda and extra free silica, so it has less alumina than most potash spars. Values are midpoints of the published ranges.
long-standing-uk-catalogue-figures-for-q: Long-standing UK catalogue figures for potash feldspar, printed by Potterycrafts, Bath Potters and CTM. Bath Potters says its potash feldspar is Norwegian.
potterycrafts-data-sheet-for-p3296-octob: Potterycrafts'' data sheet for P3296 (October 2025) gives Sibelco''s Norflux K 11 analysis instead (K₂O 11.8, Na₂O 2.9), so its current stock may be that feldspar: see Norflux Potash Feldspar.
valentine-clays-potash-feldspar-a-typica: Valentine Clays'' potash feldspar, a typical potash spar with about 10.4% K2O and 2.3% Na2O.
spanish-sodium-feldspar-albite-with-almo: Spanish sodium feldspar (albite) with almost no potash, sold by Potclays, Potterycrafts and Valentine with the same analysis. A stronger, lower-melting flux than potash feldspar.
the-soda-feldspar-figures-printed-by-pm7: The soda feldspar figures printed by Bath Potters and CTM; Bath Potters says it is Norwegian.
mixed-potash-soda-feldspar-about-7-uyikr: Mixed potash-soda feldspar (about 7% K2O, 5% Na2O) from Sibelco''s Finnish flotation plant. This is the ''FFF'' that Potclays, Potterycrafts, Valentine and CTM sell; the name stands for Finnish Flotation Feldspar.
finnish-feldspar-quartz-pegmatite-that-p: Finnish feldspar-quartz pegmatite that Potclays sells as an alternative to the now-unavailable Forshammar feldspar. Its high silica makes it behave more like Cornish stone than a true feldspar.
the-nepheline-syenite-sold-in-the-1x77jq: The nepheline syenite sold in the UK is Norwegian, with about equal K2O and Na2O. US recipes assume Canadian A270 (K2O 4.8, Na2O 10.5), so the two are not interchangeable without recalculating.
fine-dust-low-in-free-silica-1tgmsj5: Fine dust; low in free silica but avoid breathing it.
natural-cornish-stone-is-no-longer-1o4yc: Natural Cornish stone is no longer quarried, so UK suppliers now sell a substitute. Valentine''s FCS2 is ''a milled material composite flux designed to match the firing characteristics of Cornish Stone''; it melts 1100-1300 °C.
the-leadless-frit-most-used-in-r48r5w: The leadless frit most used in UK earthenware glazes: a calcium borosilicate with about 19% B2O3. Firing range 900-1050 °C (Bath Potters) or 950-1150 °C (Potclays).
not-classified-ctm-standard-borax-frit-1: Not classified (CTM Standard Borax Frit SDS 36, used as the equivalent); avoid breathing the dust.
potterycrafts-standard-borax-frit-a-gene: Potterycrafts'' standard borax frit, a general-purpose leadless frit for earthenware glazes. Expansion 8.3 x 10^-6/°C, firing range 900-1100 °C.
not-classified-potterycrafts-sds-p2953-u: Not classified (Potterycrafts SDS P2953; under 1% quartz); breathing the dust over long periods raises the risk of lung disease.
soft-fluid-high-expansion-alkaline-frit-: Soft, fluid, high-expansion alkaline frit for crackle and raku glazes and alkaline copper blues. Expansion 13.4 x 10^-6/°C, firing range 880-1060 °C.
contains-barium-about-7-bao-soluble-1xab: Contains barium (about 7% BaO); soluble alkaline frit, avoid ingestion.
newer-uk-high-alkaline-frit-with-1swirl0: Newer UK high alkaline frit with roughly equal soda and potash (about 17% each) and no barium; for crackle glazes and copper blues. Firing range 860-1060 °C.
very-soluble-alkaline-frit-avoid-ingesti: Very soluble alkaline frit; avoid ingestion.
sodium-borosilicate-frit-with-about-25-a: Sodium borosilicate frit with about 25% B2O3 and almost no lime, recommended for copper turquoise glazes. Expansion 6.9 x 10^-6/°C, firing range 900-1100 °C.
not-classified-potterycrafts-sds-p2961-b: Not classified (Potterycrafts SDS P2961); breathing the dust over long periods raises the risk of lung disease.
uk-fritted-calcium-borate-used-in-nlgcqo: UK fritted calcium borate used in place of colemanite or Gerstley borate (about 50% B2O3, 26.5% CaO). Expansion 6.1 x 10^-6/°C, firing range 1050-1160 °C. In stock at Potterycrafts in October 2026.
not-classified-potterycrafts-sds-p2954-b: Not classified (Potterycrafts SDS P2954); breathing the dust over long periods raises the risk of lung disease.
potclays-calcium-borate-frit-long-establ: Potclays'' calcium borate frit, ''long established as the substitute for colemanite in glazes''. A damp, coarse frit; firing range 800-1100 °C, not for fast firing.
not-classified-equivalent-potterycrafts-: Not classified (equivalent Potterycrafts P2954 SDS; Bath Potters'' calcium borate frit sheet says no labelling is needed); avoid breathing the dust.
ctm-s-calcium-borate-frit-on-1ttusd1: CTM''s calcium borate frit, on sale until at least 2019 and ''not available'' by December 2025. The analysis is the one CTM''s price lists printed from 2016 to 2026 (the same as Potterycrafts P2954); CTM''s frits web page gives an older one (SiO₂ 24, Al₂O₃ 8, B₂O₃ 41, CaO 22). CTM suggests, for every 100 g removed from a recipe: add 167 g Gillespie Borate and 10 g quartz, and take out 12 g whiting and 26 g potash feldspar, then test.
not-classified-ctm-sds-37-avoid-o1fm3n: Not classified (CTM SDS 37); avoid breathing the dust.
leadless-low-expansion-frit-small-additi: Leadless low-expansion frit; small additions raise a glaze''s craze resistance, large amounts give milkiness. Firing range 1020-1150 °C (Bath Potters) or 1040-1100 °C (Potclays). Potclays'' sheet, and Bath Potters after it, prints Li₂O 0.10, which leaves the analysis at 99.0%. Potclays'' own formula on the same sheet (0.176 Li₂O) gives 1.06%, as the near-identical Potterycrafts P2960 does, so 1.1 is used.
not-classified-equivalent-potterycrafts-: Not classified (equivalent Potterycrafts P2960 SDS); avoid breathing the dust.
low-expansion-borax-frit-used-to-1bguah0: Low-expansion borax frit used to cut glaze expansion where crazing is a problem; above about 5% it can dull the surface. Expansion 3.8 x 10^-6/°C, firing range 1020-1150 °C.
not-classified-potterycrafts-sds-p2960-b: Not classified (Potterycrafts SDS P2960); breathing the dust over long periods raises the risk of lung disease.
a-true-lead-bisilicate-65-66-1ics0hr: A ''true'' lead bisilicate (65-66% PbO, 32% SiO2, 2% Al2O3) still sold in the UK as the usual frit for low-solubility earthenware glazes; firing 880-1050 °C (Potclays).
lead-frit-toxic-if-the-dust-1fnhzt2: Lead frit: toxic if the dust is breathed in or swallowed. Fired glazes can release lead into food and drink; UK suppliers say low-solubility glazes are not food safe by default and ware must be metal-release tested.
higher-lead-frit-1-pbo-to-1je72om: Higher-lead frit (1 PbO to 1.5 SiO2) sold by Potclays and Bath Potters ''for artistic glazes where food safety is not required''. Firing range 860-1040 °C (Potclays).
lead-frit-toxic-if-the-dust-foqu21: Lead frit: toxic if the dust is breathed in or swallowed. Fired glazes can release lead into food and drink; UK suppliers say low-solubility glazes are not food safe by default and ware must be metal-release tested. Sold explicitly as not for food-contact ware.
uk-flint-is-calcined-flint-pebble-6yaur1: UK ''flint'' is calcined flint pebble, not ground quartz: about 96% SiO2 with 1.3% CaO and 1.3% LOI. Valentine says it raises thermal expansion when added to a glaze. US recipes that say ''flint'' mean ground quartz.
respirable-crystalline-silica-including-: Respirable crystalline silica, including some cristobalite; use a suitable respirator.
the-potash-feldspar-that-most-german-mhg: The potash feldspar that most German pottery suppliers sell (BSZ, Carl Jäger, Keramik-Kraft, Töpferbedarf Rantzau), also sold by Lehmhuus (Switzerland), keramik.at (Austria) and Solargil (France). BSZ gives it as about 72% potash feldspar, 23% soda feldspar and 2% quartz.
potterycrafts-p3296-data-sheet-october-2: Potterycrafts'' P3296 data sheet (October 2025) gives this analysis, so it appears to be sold in the UK as P3296.
sibelco-s-safety-data-sheet-2024-hx53ln: Sibelco''s safety data sheet (2024-03) does not classify it and gives fine quartz below 1%, with up to 25% nepheline syenite in the mix. Avoid breathing the dust.
albite-soda-feldspar-from-sibelco-s-d39b: Albite soda feldspar from Sibelco''s German range, sold by Carl Jäger and BSZ as ''Feldspat Na LF 90'' and by Keramik-Kraft as ''Natron (Maxum/LA75)''. It is almost pure albite, so it melts earlier than the Norflux potash feldspar.
carl-ja-ger-s-safety-data-szccqx: Carl Jäger''s safety data sheet (2012) gives 1-3% quartz; the dust can contain respirable crystalline silica. Avoid breathing it.
potash-feldspar-sold-by-the-swiss-1jyw5l: Potash feldspar sold by the Swiss pottery supplier Bodmer Ton, with about 10.7% K2O and 3% Na2O. Bodmer gives its melting point as 1250 °C.
soda-feldspar-mainly-albite-with-a-usgao: Soda feldspar (mainly albite) with a little extra quartz, sold by Bodmer Ton in Switzerland. Bodmer gives its melting point as 1180 °C.
bodmer-labels-it-ghs08-health-hazard-yp1: Bodmer labels it GHS08 (health hazard) because the dust contains respirable crystalline silica; avoid breathing it.
spanish-potash-feldspar-from-imerys-s-1v: Spanish potash feldspar from Imerys''s plant at Onda, sold by several French pottery suppliers (Ceradel, Solargil, Céram-Décor). Its chemistry is close to G-200 EU, which Imerys makes at the same plant for the US market.
imerys-s-safety-data-sheet-2013-15ms3kd: Imerys''s safety data sheet (2013) does not classify it and gives less than 1% respirable quartz; avoid breathing the dust.
very-white-potash-feldspar-mostly-orthoc: Very white potash feldspar, mostly orthoclase, sold by the French supplier Ceradel; about 5% is retained on a 44 µm sieve.
a-blend-of-feldspars-with-more-1l53rzf: A blend of feldspars with more soda (6.9%) than potash (4.3%), sold by Ceradel. It sits between a soda and a potash feldspar in melting behaviour.
spanish-soda-feldspar-sold-to-potters-uj: Spanish soda feldspar sold to potters by Prodesco and by shops that stock its range (Marphil, Kádar), and in France by Solargil as ''Feldspath sodique FN72''. Prodesco gives it as 61% albite, 7% orthoclase, 8% anorthite and 24% quartz, so it carries a lot of free silica.
about-24-quartz-by-the-supplier-da180d: About 24% quartz by the supplier''s mineral analysis, so the dust contains respirable crystalline silica; avoid breathing it.
the-potash-feldspar-of-spain-s-7emvi0: The potash feldspar of Spain''s main pottery raw-material brand. Despite its name it carries only 7.5% K2O with 3.75% Na2O and extra silica, so it is a weaker flux than a true potash spar.
a-sodic-pegmatite-soda-feldspar-with-llp: A sodic pegmatite: soda feldspar with a lot of quartz, sold to Spanish potters. It is a stiffer, more siliceous flux than soda feldspar, used somewhat like Cornish stone.
high-in-free-quartz-about-75-1feyvbz: High in free quartz (about 75% SiO2 overall); the dust contains respirable crystalline silica. Avoid breathing it.
a-very-pure-potash-feldspar-86-zztdw5: A very pure potash feldspar (86% potash feldspar, 7% soda feldspar, 5% quartz by the supplier''s mineral analysis), with 14.5% K2O and under 1% Na2O, close to ideal orthoclase. Sold to potters by Sila Argille in Italy.
swedish-feldspar-quartz-rock-from-sibelc: Swedish feldspar-quartz rock from Sibelco''s Forshammar quarry, with about equal soda and potash and much free silica. Forshammar feldspar is named in many older Swedish stoneware recipes, but Swedish and UK pottery suppliers now sell Finnish FFF or FFP 45 in its place.
high-in-free-quartz-sio2-about-1h1npth: High in free quartz (SiO2 about 76%); the dust contains respirable crystalline silica. Avoid breathing it.
washed-kaolin-from-the-old-zettlitz-1rbg: Washed kaolin from the old Zettlitz (Sedlec) pits near Karlovy Vary, more than 90% kaolinite. It was long the reference kaolin of German ceramic chemistry, so recipes that call for ''Zettlitzer Kaolin'' mean this material. Still sold to potters for glazes, engobes and porcelain.
kaolin-dust-may-contain-a-little-15eorz7: Kaolin dust; may contain a little crystalline silica (quartz). Avoid breathing the dust.
the-plain-kaolin-that-bodmer-ton-hgczzf: The plain ''Kaolin'' that Bodmer Ton, a large Swiss pottery supplier, sells alongside its English china clay. It is coarser and less plastic than Cornish china clay (only 19% finer than 2 microns) and has more silica and potash (2.9% K2O), so it adds a little flux. Used to bring alumina and silica into glazes and for white engobes.
kaolin-dust-german-washed-kaolins-usuall: Kaolin dust; German washed kaolins usually contain some fine quartz. Avoid breathing the dust.
the-standard-kaolin-of-carl-ja-4uwzzt: The standard ''Kaolin'' of Carl Jäger, a large German pottery supplier in the Westerwald. Carl Jäger describes it as very white-firing, for glazes and bodies, raising scratch hardness, chemical resistance and glaze viscosity. Glazy entries show it is also sold in Belgium (Argilières Hins), and Silica Nordic in Denmark sells a kaolin with the same figures.
carl-ja-ger-s-safety-data-a594dg: Carl Jäger''s safety data sheet (version 5, 30.01.2018) classifies it as not hazardous but notes it contains less than 1% fine crystalline silica; avoid making dust.
white-firing-breton-porcelain-kaolin-sol: White-firing Breton porcelain kaolin, sold to French potters as Kaolinor 1C (Ceradel) and to Spanish potters as Caolín d''Arvor (Prodesco). A plain, fairly pure kaolin for glazes, engobes and porcelain bodies.
ceradel-s-safety-sheet-dec-2024-ei419a: Ceradel''s safety sheet (Dec 2024) lists it as 100% kaolin, not classified as hazardous; treat the dust like any clay dust.
the-spanish-national-kaolin-that-spanish: The Spanish ''national'' kaolin that Spanish pottery shops (Prodesco, Marphil in Madrid) sell for glazes, engobes and high-fire bodies, as against imported English kaolin. Slightly more silica and less potash than Cornish or Breton kaolin.
kaolin-dust-may-contain-some-fine-14c37u: Kaolin dust; may contain some fine quartz. Avoid breathing the dust.
a-light-firing-kaolinitic-westerwald-cla: A light-firing, kaolinitic Westerwald clay (46% kaolinite, 18% mica, 25% quartz) from one of the main German clay miners, sold as milled clay powder. Its analysis and fineness are close to an English ball clay such as TWVA (about 28% alumina, 11.6% LOI), so it can stand in for one in glazes and engobes.
contains-crystalline-silica-about-25-qua: Contains crystalline silica (about 25% quartz by the maker''s mineral analysis); avoid breathing the dust.
a-german-westerwald-ball-clay-that-f3nfk: A German (Westerwald) ball clay that Sibelco lists for glazes and engobes: very fine (69% under 2 microns), light-firing, with about 24% alumina and 2.8% potash. Its analysis is close to the English HVAR ball clay.
ball-clays-contain-free-quartz-avoid-hho: Ball clays contain free quartz; avoid breathing the dust.
a-potassium-sodium-borosilicate-frit-wit: A potassium-sodium borosilicate frit with a lot of alkali, from Vibrantz''s Frankfurt range. It is the usual German frit for raku and other alkaline low-fire glazes. Expansion is 150 x 10^-7/K (20-400 °C); it starts to soften at 645 °C and reaches the half-sphere point at 740 °C.
leadless-frit-glass-cas-65997-18-16pz22p: Leadless frit (glass, CAS 65997-18-4). No SDS was found for this product. Similar leadless frits from Mondré & Manz and Reimbold & Strick are not classified as hazardous in their SDSs. Avoid breathing the dust.
a-sodium-borosilicate-frit-with-no-wufbi: A sodium borosilicate frit with no alumina. It is a strong low-temperature flux and boron source. BSZ sells it for leadless alkaline glazes, especially raku, and it also appears in crystalline-glaze recipes. Expansion is 85 x 10^-7/K; it starts to soften at 685 °C and reaches the half-sphere point at 780 °C.
leadless-frit-glass-cas-65997-18-g5r9m7: Leadless frit (glass, CAS 65997-18-4) with a lot of boron. No SDS was found for this product. Some EU suppliers label boron-rich frits as toxic to reproduction (H360FD), so check the SDS that comes with the bag. Avoid breathing the dust.
a-calcium-potassium-borosilicate-frit-so: A calcium-potassium borosilicate frit sold as a ''Basisfritte'' (base frit). With about 12% alumina, its chemistry is close to a complete glaze and suits clear earthenware and low stoneware bases. Expansion is low, 56 x 10^-7/K; it starts to soften at 865 °C and reaches the half-sphere point at 1050 °C.
a-calcium-borosilicate-frit-with-little-: A calcium borosilicate frit with little boron and about 12% alumina. Its high melting point makes it suited to stoneware and higher-fired earthenware glazes. Expansion is 76 x 10^-7/K; it starts to soften at 830 °C and reaches the half-sphere point at about 1080 °C. Sold by Hans Wolbring, keramikbedarf-online.de and Lehmhuus (Switzerland).
a-zinc-barium-silicate-frit-with-gmr2om: A zinc-barium silicate frit with no boron, used for satin-matte and matte glazes and as a less soluble way to add barium and zinc. Expansion is about 103-105 x 10^-7/K; it starts to soften at 835 °C and reaches the half-sphere point at 990 °C. Sold by BSZ, Hans Wolbring and keramikbedarf-online.de.
leadless-but-it-contains-about-35-ok0uml: Leadless, but it contains about 35% barium oxide and 19% zinc oxide bound in glass. No SDS was found. Barium in a frit is much less soluble than barium carbonate, but test any barium glaze for leaching before it is used on food surfaces. Avoid breathing the dust.
a-low-expansion-sodium-borosilicate-frit: A low-expansion sodium borosilicate frit: high in silica and boron, with little alkali. Low-expansion frits like this one are added to glazes to lower their thermal expansion and cure crazing. On its own it melts only at high temperature (half-sphere point 1270 °C). Expansion is 48 x 10^-7/K. Sold by Hans Wolbring and keramikbedarf-online.de.
a-calcium-alkali-borosilicate-frit-with-: A calcium-alkali borosilicate frit with about 11% alumina, sold as an ''Alkaliborfritte''. keramikbedarf-online.de sells it for the resist layer in naked raku and as a flux in aventurine glazes. Expansion is 65 x 10^-7/K; it starts to soften at 830 °C and reaches the half-sphere point at 970 °C.
a-soda-potash-lime-frit-with-52qvc2: A soda-potash-lime frit with no boron and almost no alumina. Its expansion is very high: 141 x 10^-7/K, with softening at 503 °C. It is used for raku, crackle and crystalline glazes and for strong alkaline blues and turquoises. Sold by Carl Jäger, BSZ, Keramik-Kraft, Hans Wolbring, Rantzauer Töpferbedarf and Ing. Lehrer (Austria).
leadless-frit-glass-cas-65997-18-1h3mmym: Leadless frit (glass, CAS 65997-18-4). The SDS supplied by Carl Jäger for this Mondré & Manz frit says it is not classified as hazardous under CLP. Avoid breathing the dust.
a-zinc-alkali-borosilicate-frit-rich-1ia: A zinc alkali borosilicate frit, rich in potash, with high expansion: 108 x 10^-7/K, softening at 582 °C. It is sold for matte, satin and crackle glazes and for raising a glaze''s expansion. Sold by Carl Jäger, BSZ and Rantzauer Töpferbedarf.
a-leadless-alkali-frit-containing-lithiu: A leadless alkali frit containing lithium, zinc and calcium. Suppliers describe it as a gloss frit, opacified by boron, with high surface tension, for clear, white and effect glazes. Expansion is 65.9 x 10^-7/K, with softening at 680 °C. Sold by Carl Jäger, BSZ and Rantzauer Töpferbedarf.
a-leadless-borosilicate-frit-opacified-w: A leadless borosilicate frit opacified with zircon (7.5% ZrO2), for white glazes. It was developed for fast-fired earthenware wall tiles. Expansion is 63 x 10^-7/K, with softening at 690 °C. Sold by Carl Jäger and Rantzauer Töpferbedarf.
a-leadless-sodium-borosilicate-frit-sold: A leadless sodium borosilicate frit sold for raku glazes. Suppliers also suggest it for celadons and, with added iron oxide, for aventurine glazes. Expansion is 72.8 x 10^-7/K (20-400 °C), with softening at 565 °C. Sold by Keramik-Kraft and Rantzauer Töpferbedarf.
a-calcium-borate-frit-with-very-cmvn8f: A calcium borate frit with very little silica, used as a concentrated source of boron and calcium. German suppliers sell it as a replacement for colemanite and Portabor that avoids their thickening of the slurry and their spitting in the kiln. Expansion is 76.2 x 10^-7/K, with softening at 670 °C. Sold by keramikbedarf-online.de and Rantzauer Töpferbedarf.
a-barium-zinc-frit-that-contains-5y8sr8: A barium-zinc frit that contains 11% lead oxide; the maker lists it among its lead frits. Keramik-Kraft sells it simply as ''Zinkbarium Fritte''. It is used for matte and crystalline glaze effects. Expansion is 119 x 10^-7/K, with softening above 870 °C.
contains-lead-pbo-about-11-and-1wywyyz: CONTAINS LEAD (PbO about 11%) and barium (BaO about 38%). Keramik-Kraft lists H351 (suspected of causing cancer), H360FD (may damage fertility or the unborn child), H362 (may harm breast-fed children), H372 (damages organs through prolonged exposure) and H410 (very toxic to aquatic life). It is not suitable for schools or hobby use without proper controls. Lab-test any glaze made with it for lead and barium release before it is used on food or drink surfaces.
a-low-expansion-calcium-borosilicate-fri: A low-expansion calcium borosilicate frit: expansion 42 x 10^-7/K, transformation 650 °C, softening 710 °C. Keramik-Kraft sells it as ''Calziumborat Fritte'' and as a replacement for colemanite. It has far less boron and far more silica than a true calcium borate frit.
leadless-frit-cas-65997-18-4-s12mq5: Leadless frit (CAS 65997-18-4). The Reimbold & Strick SDS seen for a similar leadless frit (A 3249 P, 2017) does not classify it as hazardous. Avoid breathing the dust.
a-calcium-borate-frit-with-one-awae2q: A calcium borate frit with one CaO to one B2O3 and no silica or alumina; Dutch recipes call it ''calciumboraatfritte 3221''. It is a concentrated boron source, chemically like colemanite without the water. Sold by Keramikos, Cock Keramiek, Ve-Ka and De Beeldhouwwinkel.
leadless-keramikos-and-ve-ka-state-ngetf: Leadless. Keramikos and Ve-Ka state that it is not classified as hazardous under CLP. Avoid breathing the dust.
a-zinc-borosilicate-frit-with-no-ua13zq: A zinc borosilicate frit with no alumina and about 29% ZnO. Dutch recipes use it to add zinc in fritted form, for matte, crystalline and zinc-dependent colour effects. Sold by Keramikos and Cock Keramiek.
leadless-keramikos-and-cock-keramiek-sta: Leadless. Keramikos and Cock Keramiek state that it is not classified as hazardous. Avoid breathing the dust.
a-sodium-zinc-alkali-frit-with-o6mq1u: A sodium-zinc alkali frit with no boron and little alumina: the classic Dutch ''alkalifritte 1510'' for alkaline glazes such as turquoise copper blues, raku and crackle. Keramikos and Ve-Ka (as ''Alkali 2495'') still sell it in 2026. Keramikos now also sells ''Alkali fritte 21.20'' as its replacement.
leadless-keramikos-states-that-it-is-6gm: Leadless. Keramikos states that it is not classified as hazardous under CLP. Avoid breathing the dust.
standard-lead-bisilicate-frit-pbo-2sio2-: Standard lead bisilicate frit (PbO·2SiO2 with a little alumina) for low-fired earthenware and majolica glazes; it is the Dutch counterpart of UK lead bisilicate. Sold by Cock Keramiek, Ve-Ka (as 3647) and De Beeldhouwwinkel (Keramikos 10.05).
contains-lead-pbo-about-65-cock-7wgj88: CONTAINS LEAD (PbO about 65%). Cock Keramiek marks it ''Gevaarlijke stof''. Lead frits are classified in the EU as Repr. 1A and STOT RE 1. Reimbold & Strick''s SDS for its lead frit A 1316 P lists: H302+H332 (harmful if swallowed or inhaled), H351 (suspected of causing cancer), H360Df (may damage the unborn child; suspected of damaging fertility), H372 (damages organs through prolonged exposure) and H410 (very toxic to aquatic life). Use it only with dust control, gloves and good hygiene, and keep it away from children and food areas. Lab-test any glaze made with it for lead release before it is used on food or drink surfaces.
lead-monosilicate-frit-one-pbo-to-yl6thf: Lead monosilicate frit (one PbO to one SiO2), the most lead-rich standard frit. It is a very strong low-temperature flux for earthenware and raku glazes. Expansion is about 89-90 x 10^-7/K, with softening at about 450-470 °C. Sold to potters by Ve-Ka (Netherlands, as 2994). Ing. Lehrer (Austria) publishes the 2019 SDS for R&S A 1316 P.
contains-lead-pbo-about-79-reimbold-t25l: CONTAINS LEAD (PbO about 79%). Reimbold & Strick''s SDS for A 1316 P (rev. 1.07, 2019) classifies it as Repr. 1A and STOT RE 1: H302+H332 (harmful if swallowed or inhaled), H351 (suspected of causing cancer), H360Df (may damage the unborn child; suspected of damaging fertility), H372 (damages organs through prolonged exposure) and H410 (very toxic to aquatic life). Use it only with dust control, gloves and good hygiene. Lab-test any glaze made with it for lead release before it is used on food or drink surfaces.
water-washed-primary-kaolin-from-pittong: Water-washed primary kaolin from Pittong near Ballarat, Australia''s only hydrous kaolin plant; the standard Australian china clay for glazes and white bodies. Sold by Walker Ceramics (BA330), Pottery Supplies Online, The Potter''s Market and others.
sds-suvo-minerals-australia-eckalite-1-1: SDS (Suvo Minerals Australia, Eckalite 1 & 1 Plus, 2024): kaolin >98%, crystalline silica (quartz) <1%. Avoid breathing the dust.
a-second-pittong-kaolin-grade-slightly-1: A second Pittong kaolin grade, slightly more iron-bearing than Eckalite 1; sold to potters by Walker Ceramics (BA331, which replaced their Eckaglas), Northcote Pottery Supplies and Blackwattle Pottery. Used for glaze alumina, suspension and slips. Walker''s figures are the ones it gave in 2007 for Eckaglas, the grade this replaced.
kaolin-the-related-eckalite-1-sds-57l3rd: Kaolin; the related Eckalite 1 SDS (2024) gives quartz <1%. Avoid breathing the dust.
very-white-low-iron-low-titania-1uwzzja: Very white, low-iron, low-titania halloysite (a kaolin-group clay) separated from altered rhyolite at Matauri Bay; used for translucent porcelain and very clear glazes. Sold in Australia by Walker Ceramics (BA139) and in the US as ''Kaolin New Zealand''.
kaolin-group-clay-with-fine-tubular-1t37: Kaolin-group clay with fine tubular particles; the parent rock is quartz and cristobalite and traces may remain (the brochure''s XRD shows both). Avoid breathing the dust.
dry-milled-very-plastic-secondary-clay-7: Dry-milled, very plastic secondary clay from Claypro''s own pit at Axedale, Victoria; the Australian ball clay sold to potters as CA1 (Northcote) and CA2 (Walker, Blackwattle). Used for plasticity in bodies and for suspension, silica and alumina in glazes.
claypro-sds-2015-about-20-crystalline-2r: Claypro SDS (2015): about 20% crystalline silica (quartz); classified Carcinogen Category 1A (H350, by inhalation). Avoid breathing the dust.
a-plastic-white-firing-kaolinitic-clay-1: A plastic, white-firing kaolinitic clay with ball-clay working properties, made to replace the older Cresta BB and BB4; it appears in older Australian recipes as ''Clay Ceram''. Walker Ceramics marks it ''no longer available''.
walker-ceramics-already-listed-it-as-1ni: Walker Ceramics already listed it as no longer available in October 2016.
unimin-tds-contains-free-crystalline-sil: Unimin TDS: contains free crystalline silica (quartz). Avoid breathing the dust.
a-thai-potash-feldspar-of-the-1yw5cs8: A Thai potash feldspar of the kind now sold as ''potash feldspar'' in Australia; Walker Ceramics lists its BA350 as Thai and Blackwattle''s SDS names ''Potash Feldspar K200BL'' (Scott Chemicals). Main high-temperature flux for stoneware and porcelain glazes. The analysis is Sibelco''s; that Australian shops'' Thai potash feldspar is this K200 is inferred from its name and origin.
sds-for-potash-feldspar-k200bl-scott-190: SDS for Potash Feldspar K200BL (Scott Chemicals, 2021): feldspar 90-98%, quartz 2-10%. Avoid breathing the dust.
albite-type-soda-feldspar-imported-from-: Albite-type soda feldspar imported from India and sold by Walker Ceramics and Blackwattle Pottery; a glossier, slightly lower-melting flux than potash feldspar for stoneware and mid-fire glazes. Walker''s figures date from 2007 and give no calcium, which Indian soda feldspars usually have.
walker-msds-2019-soda-feldspar-98-1phdzl: Walker MSDS (2019): soda feldspar >98%, with quartz listed as a hazardous component. Avoid breathing the dust.
walker-s-fluorine-free-blend-of-1i67hb4: Walker''s fluorine-free blend of minerals made to match natural Cornish stone; Walker describes it as a slightly weaker flux than feldspar, for recipes that call for Cornish stone. Also sold by Pottery Supplies Online and, as ''Cornish Stone (Sub Blend)'', by Keane Ceramics. Walker prints 1.5% iron oxide, high for a Cornish stone substitute; check with Walker before relying on it.
no-sds-reviewed-as-a-feldspar-19nqyax: No SDS reviewed. As a feldspar and quartz type blend it will contain crystalline silica; avoid breathing the dust.
milled-quartz-flour-about-90-finer-lnsq1: Milled quartz flour (about 90% finer than 45 microns) from Sibelco''s Lang Lang operation; the ''Silica 200#'' sold by Walker (BA770), Keane, Northcote and Blackwattle. Walker''s SDS names the Sibelco WQ series.
sibelco-sds-milled-silica-products-2011-: Sibelco SDS (milled silica products, 2011): quartz 99%, more than 20% respirable crystalline silica. Prolonged inhalation causes silicosis and lung cancer; avoid breathing the dust.
lead-free-high-soda-high-expansion-4gjtq: Lead-free, high-soda, high-expansion frit with a little boron. It was Ferro Australia''s counterpart of US Frit 3110 and is named in many Australian recipes for copper turquoise, manganese purple and crackle glazes (Walker gives 980-1080°C, expansion 96 x10^-7). Walker Ceramics now supplies imported US Ferro 3110 in its place, and some shops still sell under the 4110 name, so check which frit you have.
walker-ceramics-listed-it-until-february: Walker Ceramics listed it until February 2020, but no longer by March 2021.
no-sds-seen-frit-is-a-t89ijb: No SDS seen. Frit is a ground glass with no free crystalline silica; avoid breathing the fine dust.
lead-free-calcium-borosilicate-frit-ferr: Lead-free calcium borosilicate frit, Ferro Australia''s version of US Frit 3124 but with less alumina. It is a common base for earthenware glazes, including clear glazes over underglaze, at 1040-1100°C (Walker; expansion 74 x10^-7). Australian and NZ suppliers now sell US Ferro 3124 as its replacement; 3124 has more alumina, so a recipe written for 4124 may need a little less kaolin.
soft-lead-free-high-calcium-borosilicate: Soft, lead-free, high-calcium borosilicate frit. It was Ferro Australia''s counterpart of US Frit 3134, with a little alumina, and it appears in many older Australian earthenware and mid-fire recipes. Suppliers now sell US Ferro 3134 in its place, and Walker suggests 60% 3134-2 with 40% 3124 to imitate 4108.
medium-hard-lead-free-calcium-sodium-1da: Medium-hard, lead-free calcium-sodium borosilicate frit for clear glazes. Ferro described a glaze of the frit plus 10% kaolin as firing 1050-1100°C (Walker gives expansion 61 x10^-7). Walker reports that Ferro suggested US Frit 3124 as the closest replacement after 4131 was discontinued.
hard-lead-free-clear-borosilicate-frit-1: Hard, lead-free, clear borosilicate frit for earthenware at 1040-1100°C (Walker; expansion 69 x10^-7). It is named in older Australian recipes. Walker replaced it with 4131, which has itself been discontinued, so US Frit 3124 is now the nearest frit on sale.
alumina-free-lead-free-sodium-calcium-4v: Alumina-free, lead-free sodium-calcium borosilicate frit for earthenware at 1040-1100°C (Walker; expansion 83 x10^-7). No supplier names a replacement. US Frit 3134 is the nearest one on sale, though it has more calcium and less sodium.
standard-low-solubility-lead-bisilicate-: Standard low-solubility lead bisilicate frit (about 65% lead oxide) for bright, glossy earthenware glazes at 950-1050°C (Walker; expansion 72 x10^-7). It is sold in Australia as 4064 or 3531 by Walker Ceramics, Keane Ceramics, NR Pottery Supplies, Ipswich Pottery Supplies and Blackwattle Pottery (''Frit 3531 (replaces 4064)'').
lead-frit-about-65-lead-oxide-1r8qgke: LEAD FRIT: about 65% lead oxide, held in glass. Lead compounds are toxic if swallowed or inhaled, can harm fertility and the unborn child, and damage organs with repeated exposure. Avoid all dust, wear a P2/P3 respirator, wash after use, and keep it away from food areas and children. Glazes made with it must be correctly formulated and fired, and lead release from functional ware should be tested by a laboratory.
dense-lead-free-zircon-opacified-white-1: Dense, lead-free, zircon-opacified white frit (about 12% ZrO2) for white and pastel earthenware glazes at 1040-1100°C (Walker; expansion 59 x10^-7). Walker Ceramics has sold Frit 9113 in its place since 2022 (listed for a time as 9117), but no analysis of 9113 is published.
no-sds-seen-frit-is-a-btjxa5: No SDS seen. Frit is a ground glass with no free crystalline silica. It contains zirconium and zinc oxides in the glass. Avoid breathing the fine dust.
a-leadless-very-low-expansion-calcium-zq: A leadless, very low-expansion calcium-barium borosilicate frit (expansion 40 x 10^-7/K), high in silica and boron. Frits this low in expansion are added in small amounts to lower a glaze''s expansion and cure crazing. On its own it is stiff (softening 910 °C, half-sphere point 1280 °C). Sold by Hans Wolbring (Höhr-Grenzhausen, Germany).
leadless-frit-glass-cas-65997-18-1jelw38: Leadless frit (glass, CAS 65997-18-4) with about 6% barium oxide and 22% boron oxide bound in the glass. No SDS was found for this product. Some EU suppliers label boron-rich frits as toxic to reproduction (H360FD), so check the SDS that comes with the bag. Avoid breathing the dust.
a-leadless-calcium-zinc-borosilicate-fri: A leadless calcium-zinc borosilicate frit with a little lithium and barium, sold for matte to satin-matte effect glazes. Expansion is 70 x 10^-7/K; transformation 555 °C, softening 740 °C, half-sphere point 970 °C. Sold by BSZ Keramikbedarf (which names Vibrantz GmbH, Frankfurt, as maker) and Hans Wolbring.
leadless-frit-glass-cas-65997-18-14d0cts: Leadless frit (glass, CAS 65997-18-4) with about 6% barium oxide and 7% zinc oxide bound in the glass. No SDS was found for this product. Barium in a frit is much less soluble than barium carbonate, but test any barium glaze for leaching before it is used on food surfaces. Avoid breathing the dust.
chromium-iii-oxide-about-99-cr2o3-1xoqx1: Chromium(III) oxide, about 99% Cr2O3: a very strong, refractory green colorant (it melts at about 2435 C / 4415 F). In oxidizing firings from about cone 6 up a little chromium vaporizes and can flash pink onto nearby tin-opacified glazes; with zinc it turns brown.
not-classified-no-signal-word-on-md0bl8: Not classified (no signal word) on the Potterycrafts and Laguna/Huntsman SDSs; some EU notifiers add H317 (may cause skin allergy). Contains traces of hexavalent chromium (under 100 ppm), and heating in air can form a little more, so avoid breathing the dust and kiln fumes.
black-cobalt-oxide-mostly-co3o4-sold-o5x: Black cobalt oxide, mostly Co₃O₄, sold as about 71–73% cobalt: in a glaze it counts as about 92.7% CoO, with about 6.3% oxygen lost in firing (Potterycrafts lists 95% Co₃O₄, 4% CoO and 0.9% NiO as the main impurity). Gives up that oxygen to become CoO at about 900–950 C (1650–1740 F) in air, lower in reduction. About 1.6 times as strong as cobalt carbonate (93% CoO against 58%). A very strong blue: 0.25% gives a clear blue, 1–1.5% a deep blue-black.
danger-potterycrafts-sds-h334-may-cause-: Danger (Potterycrafts SDS): H334 may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled; H412 harmful to aquatic life. Laguna''s US SDS adds H302 harmful if swallowed, H317 skin sensitizer and H351 suspected of causing cancer; some EU SDSs list H350i (may cause cancer by inhalation). Avoid breathing the dust.
a-pink-purple-basic-cobalt-carbonate-1xj: A pink-purple basic cobalt carbonate with 45–47% cobalt, so about 58% CoO; the rest (about 42%) burns off as CO2 and water. It disperses more evenly than cobalt oxide; use about 1.5 times as much for the same blue.
danger-potterycrafts-sds-matching-the-eu: Danger (Potterycrafts SDS, matching the EU harmonised classification): H302 harmful if swallowed; H332 harmful if inhaled; H317 may cause an allergic skin reaction; H334 may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled; H341 suspected of causing genetic defects; H350i may cause cancer by inhalation; H360F may damage fertility; H400/H410 very toxic to aquatic life.
black-copper-oxide-cuo-about-98-1hdqa68: Black copper oxide, CuO, about 98% pure (78–79% copper). Melts at about 1326 C (2419 F), but in air first loses oxygen to Cu₂O from about 1010–1030 C. A strong, active flux that can make glazes run; copper becomes increasingly volatile above about 1025 C (1877 F) and can flash onto nearby ware, especially tin whites. Coarser than the carbonate, so it can speckle. Over about 5% can give black metallic surfaces unsuitable for food ware.
warning-potterycrafts-sds-h400-very-toxi: Warning (Potterycrafts SDS): H400 very toxic to aquatic life; the EU harmonised classification is H400 and H410. US SDSs (Laguna, from Phibro) give H302 harmful if swallowed. Copper fumes from hot kilns cause metal fume fever; vent the kiln.
basic-copper-carbonate-a-green-powder-sh: Basic copper carbonate, a green powder with 55–57% copper, so about 70% CuO; the rest (about 30%) leaves as CO₂ and water from about 290 C (554 F). It does not melt. Gives more even color than black copper oxide. An active flux; fumes from about 815 C (1500 F) and can flash onto nearby ware, especially tin whites.
warning-ceramic-color-chemical-sds-00909: Warning (Ceramic Color & Chemical SDS 00909-A, 2024-09, sold through The Ceramic Shop): H302 harmful if swallowed; H332 harmful if inhaled; H319 causes serious eye irritation; H400/H410 very toxic to aquatic life.
a-natural-source-of-iron-and-14y8gh2: A natural source of iron and titanium in glazes.
not-classified-ctm-sds-31-32-7ac3hh: Not classified (CTM SDS 31/32; under 0.1% quartz); avoid breathing the dust.
magnetite-fe3o4-also-sold-as-magnetic-1j: Magnetite, Fe₃O₄, also sold as magnetic iron oxide; some grades are ground natural ore containing quartz. Older potters’ books list black iron as FeO, but ferrous oxide is not sold as a potter’s material. Gram for gram it gives about as much iron as red iron oxide. A strong flux in reduction. Often coarser than red iron oxide; sieve or ball-mill it to avoid specks.
not-classified-ctm-sds-66-avoid-17wgk3h: Not classified (CTM SDS 66); avoid breathing the dust.
a-hydrated-form-of-iron-oxide-1pqopi1: A hydrated form of iron oxide. Insoluble in water, very fine particles.
not-classified-ctm-sds-73-synthetic-1e8x: Not classified (CTM SDS 73, synthetic yellow iron oxide); avoid breathing the dust.
a-material-with-hydrated-iron-oxide-1kzy: A material with hydrated iron oxide and clay. Sometimes called limonite (as a mineral of iron oxide). Many also have manganese.
danger-new-riverside-ochre-sds-natural-1: Danger (New Riverside Ochre SDS): natural ochre with 20–29% quartz (carcinogen category 1A by inhalation; can cause silicosis) and 1.5–4% manganese dioxide; avoid breathing the dust.
potters-manganese-dioxide-is-ground-ore-: Potters’ manganese dioxide is ground ore, typically about 75% MnO₂ with iron oxide, silica and alumina, so it gives only about 61% MnO. Loses oxygen in stages as it heats, to Mn₂O₃ at about 450–600 C and Mn₃O₄ at about 750–1100 C; the gas can cause bubbles. Browns, and purples in alkaline glazes; a flux once dissolved in the melt. Manganese fumes at high temperatures, so vent the kiln.
warning-potterycrafts-sds-also-laguna-pr: Warning (Potterycrafts SDS; also Laguna/Prince BrickOx SDS; EU harmonised): H302 harmful if swallowed; H332 harmful if inhaled. Ore grades may also contain crystalline silica. Manganese fumes at high temperatures, so vent the kiln.
green-nickel-oxide-is-stoichiometric-nio: Green nickel oxide is stoichiometric NiO, 78.5% nickel. It does not decompose or melt in the kiln (NiO melts at about 1955 C / 3550 F) and is refractory, so use small amounts; it gives muted greens, browns and greys, and blues or pinks in some bases.
danger-laguna-nickel-oxide-sds-ghs-1vgqp: Danger (Laguna nickel oxide SDS, GHS version 06/15): H317 may cause an allergic skin reaction; H334 may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled; H350 may cause cancer (EU: H350i, by inhalation); H372 causes lung damage through prolonged or repeated inhalation; H413 may cause long-lasting harm to aquatic life.
black-nickel-oxide-is-nio-with-kerajy: Black nickel oxide is NiO with a little extra oxygen (about 76.4–77.6% nickel), not true Ni2O3. It loses that oxygen and becomes green NiO at about 600–700 C (1100–1300 F), so in a glaze it behaves like green nickel oxide, giving about 2% less NiO per gram.
danger-laguna-nickel-oxide-sds-ghs-wakl3: Danger (Laguna nickel oxide SDS, GHS version 06/15, which names calcined black nickel oxide grades A and F): H317 may cause an allergic skin reaction; H334 may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled; H350 may cause cancer (EU: H350i, by inhalation); H372 causes lung damage through prolonged or repeated inhalation; H413 may cause long-lasting harm to aquatic life.
pr6o11-the-dark-brown-form-that-n56z4j: Pr₆O₁₁, the dark brown form that is sold. Counted here as Pr₂O₃, the form praseodymium takes in a glaze; the extra oxygen (3.1%) and up to 1% moisture count as loss on ignition. Does not melt in a kiln (about 2183 C); the 931 C often quoted is for the metal. A weak colorant: 5–8% gives lime to yellow greens, and it is mostly used in zircon-praseodymium yellow stains.
low-hazard-but-sdss-disagree-fujifilm-d1: Low hazard, but SDSs disagree: Fujifilm Wako (2023) not hazardous under GHS; LTS (2023) Warning, H315, H319, H335 (skin, eye and respiratory irritation). Most ECHA notifiers do not classify praseodymium oxide.
natural-rutile-milled-for-ceramics-about: Natural rutile milled for ceramics: about 95% TiO2 with small amounts of silica, zircon, vanadium, iron and chromium. Current US and UK grades have under 1% iron oxide, not the 9–10% often assumed. Used for tan to brown variegation, opacity and crystal growth, and with cobalt, copper or iron for broken colours.
tam-ceramics-sds-2018-warning-eye-1yrsyy: TAM Ceramics SDS (2018): Warning, eye and skin irritant (Category 2; H319, H315); dust may irritate the airways. Potterycrafts SDS: not classified. The EU''s Carc. 2 listing for inhaled TiO2 powder was annulled (2022, upheld 2025).
tio2-added-at-about-2-10-wa6in9: TiO₂. Added at about 2–10% (4% is typical) for variegation, opacity and crystal growth, and with iron or cobalt for broken colors. Also in the materials list as Titanium Oxide, for recipes that count it in the base.
vanadium-pentoxide-v2o5-an-orange-yellow: Vanadium pentoxide, V2O5, an orange-yellow powder, about 99% pure. It melts at 690 C (1274 F) and acts as a flux; alone it gives weak yellows to browns, and with tin oxide or zircon stronger yellows. Highly toxic: wear a respirator, avoid dust and vent the kiln.
danger-eu-gb-harmonised-classification-h: Danger. EU/GB harmonised classification: H301 toxic if swallowed, H330 fatal if inhaled, H335 respiratory irritation, H341 suspected of causing genetic defects, H350 may cause cancer, H361fd fertility and unborn child, H362 harm to breast-fed children, H372 lung damage from repeated exposure, H411 toxic to aquatic life. US SDSs give a slightly milder but still serious set (H302+H332, H319, H335, H341, H351, H361, H372, H411).
stannic-oxide-sno2-about-99-5-14e5t2w: Stannic oxide, SnO₂, about 99.5% pure. Does not melt at glaze temperatures (it melts at about 1630 C / 2966 F); it stays suspended as fine particles, which makes the glaze opaque: 4–6% gives a semi-opaque white, 8–10% full opacity, and a warm white in low-fired majolica. Opacifies poorly in reduction and at cone 10, where it starts to dissolve. Helps develop copper reds in reduction; with a trace of chrome it turns pink.
not-classified-no-signal-word-on-n0mh1: Not classified (no signal word) on current SDSs (Potterycrafts 2025, Laguna 2014). Breathing the dust for years can cause stannosis, a benign lung condition.
zirconium-dioxide-zro2-zirconia-rarely-u: Zirconium dioxide, ZrO₂ (zirconia). Rarely used raw in glazes: most recipes call for zircon (Zircopax, Superpax), which is zirconium silicate. Insoluble; opacifies as it stays unmelted at glaze temperatures, stiffens the melt and can reduce crazing.
not-classified-ati-zirconium-oxide-sds-1: Not classified (ATI zirconium oxide SDS, EU); avoid breathing the dust.
zirconium-silicate-zrsio4-67-2-zro2-i6z2: Zirconium silicate, ZrSiO₄: 67.2% ZrO₂ and 32.8% SiO₂. Sold as Zircopax, Superpax, Excelopax, Ultrox and Zircosil, which differ mainly in particle size. The usual opacifier: about 4–7% for semi-opaque, 8–15% or more for full opacity; 1–3% mainly hardens the glaze. Works in reduction, unlike tin oxide. Its silica counts toward the glaze.
not-classified-ctm-zirconium-silicate-sd: Not classified (CTM zirconium silicate SDS 29; under 0.01% respirable crystalline silica); slightly radioactive (uranium 285–343 ppm, thorium 116–157 ppm), so avoid breathing the dust.
synthetic-red-iron-oxide-is-about-1i5e3s: Synthetic red iron oxide is about 99% Fe₂O₃; natural red iron oxides (ground hematite) are weaker, about 76–95% Fe₂O₃ with clay, quartz and carbonate. A refractory stabilizer in oxidation until about cone 7–8, where it starts to lose oxygen and becomes a flux; in reduction it turns to FeO early and is a strong flux.
synthetic-grade-not-classified-as-hazard: Synthetic grade: not classified as hazardous (Potterycrafts SDS P3441, rev 2025-10). Natural ore grades are labelled Warning, H373 (lung damage from prolonged inhalation) because they contain respirable quartz.
wyoming-sodium-bentonite-the-standard-gl: Wyoming sodium bentonite, the standard glaze suspender; 1–3% keeps a glaze from settling, but more makes it slow to dry and prone to crawling. It adds a little iron, soda and magnesia.
danger-h350-may-cause-cancer-by-qzjuvp: Danger: H350 may cause cancer (by inhalation) and H372 causes lung damage through prolonged or repeated exposure, because it contains crystalline silica (Volclay 325: quartz up to 6%, cristobalite up to 2%). Avoid breathing dust.
a-water-washed-white-firing-smectite-11s: A water-washed, white-firing smectite clay (magnesium aluminium silicate) used at 1–2% as a glaze suspender and hardener and as a plasticizer for porcelain and other non-plastic bodies. Hydrate it fully in water before adding the other materials. Vanderbilt publishes no oxide analysis for grade T; this is regular VEEGUM''s, quoted in a 1964 patent, so treat it as approximate. It is magnesium-rich (MgO 13.7%), unlike sodium bentonite.
not-classified-vanderbilt-sds-2023-no-17: Not classified (Vanderbilt SDS 2023): no signal word. Avoid breathing dust; prolonged inhalation may cause lung injury.
a-purified-hectorite-magnesium-lithium-s: A purified hectorite (magnesium-lithium smectite) clay, now sold as Elementis Bentone MA; it suspends glazes and hardens the dry coat without slowing drying as much as CMC. Unlike bentonite it brings magnesia, lime and a little lithia rather than alumina and iron.
not-classified-elementis-sds-2016-not-j7: Not classified (Elementis SDS 2016): not a hazardous substance under GHS. Avoid breathing dust.
an-organic-gum-that-binds-and-pg9ere: An organic gum that binds and hardens the dry glaze coat, slows drying and helps brushing; it burns away in firing and is left out of the chemistry. Solutions spoil, so make small batches or add a preservative.
warning-may-form-combustible-dust-concen: Warning: may form combustible dust concentrations in air (OSHA combustible dust). No health hazard classification.
a-soluble-salt-used-in-tiny-1g4n6wq: A soluble salt used in tiny amounts to flocculate (thicken) a glaze slurry so it stays suspended; it is a process adjustment, not really a glaze ingredient. Most of its weight is water and sulfate, which leave during firing.
not-classified-giles-chemical-sds-2020-1: Not classified (Giles Chemical SDS 2020): not a hazardous substance under GHS.
manganese-ii-carbonate-a-pinkish-tan-nrm: Manganese(II) carbonate, a pinkish-tan powder; commercial grades are about 44% manganese (pure MnCO3 is 47.8%). Counted as MnO, about 57% MnO with about 43% loss on ignition as it gives off CO2 from about 200 C; gives browns, and purples to plum in alkaline glazes.
danger-h372-causes-damage-to-organs-18gj: Danger: H372, causes damage to organs (nervous system) through prolonged or repeated inhalation (Laguna SDS, rev. 2014-03; also the most common ECHA notification). Avoid the dust and vent the kiln.
basic-nickel-carbonate-a-light-green-14r: Basic nickel carbonate, a light green powder sold at about 46% nickel. Counted as NiO, about 58.5% NiO with about 41.5% loss on ignition; the gas it gives off can blister glazes. Gives muted greens, greys and browns, and is used to soften cobalt blues.
danger-h302-h332-harmful-if-swallowed-1l: Danger: H302+H332 harmful if swallowed or inhaled; H315; H317 skin sensitiser; H334 respiratory sensitiser; H341; H350i may cause cancer by inhalation; H360 may damage fertility or the unborn child; H372. EU harmonised classification adds H400/H410 (aquatic). Avoid all dust.
sold-to-potters-as-ground-natural-1ijf67: Sold to potters as ground natural chromite ore from South Africa, not a true chromate: about 46% Cr2O3 and 26% FeO, with alumina and magnesia. Very refractory; gives greys, browns with zinc, pinks to reds with tin, and blacks with cobalt.
not-classified-under-ghs-vibrantz-iron-h: Not classified under GHS (Vibrantz ''Iron Chromite Chromox 7901'' SDS, rev. 2023-01, as sold by Sounding Stone; also Prince Minerals SDS for Laguna). Avoid breathing the dust; older potters'' references call it highly toxic.
a-rare-earth-oxide-used-as-1yx4z2x: A rare-earth oxide used as a low-temperature opacifier and a weak colorant, giving cream to tan-yellow or orange especially with titanium or rutile. It settles quickly, so the glaze needs a suspender.
not-classified-pace-sds-2025-not-1ao5xnh: Not classified (PACE SDS 2025): not a hazardous substance under GHS. Some suppliers list eye, skin and respiratory irritation (H315, H319, H335). Avoid breathing dust.
natural-red-iron-oxide-mined-at-767hen: Natural red iron oxide mined at Tierga, Spain: about 87% Fe2O3 with some silica, dolomite and mica, so gram for gram it is a little weaker than synthetic red iron oxide. Bright orange-red raw; contains some soluble salts.
warning-h373-may-cause-damage-to-1vkarkk: Warning: H373, may cause damage to the lungs through prolonged or repeated inhalation, because it contains respirable quartz (Promindsa Micronox R series SDS, rev. 2015-01, distributed by Laguna).
fine-silicon-carbide-about-600-mesh-vaaz: Fine silicon carbide (about 600 mesh, FFF) gives local reduction in oxidation firings, for example copper reds; larger amounts or coarser grits make bubbly, cratered surfaces. It is left out of the chemistry, though fully burnt it would turn into about 1.5 times its weight of silica.
danger-h350-may-cause-cancer-by-15vqfe: Danger: H350 may cause cancer (by inhalation), because of a trace of crystalline silica (Washington Mills SDS 2025). Older supplier SDSs also list skin, eye and respiratory irritation (H315, H319, H335). Avoid breathing dust.
commercial-stains-are-pre-fired-insolubl: Commercial stains are pre-fired, insoluble pigments; their make-up is proprietary and they colour the glass by staying suspended in it, so they are left out of the chemistry. Check the maker''s notes for each stain: some need no zinc, some need high calcium, and each has a maximum firing temperature.
varies-by-stain-check-the-sds-rfi082: Varies by stain: check the SDS for the specific stain. Mason''s SDSs list many stains (e.g. 6600 Best Black) as not classified, but stains can contain cobalt, nickel, chromium, manganese, vanadium, praseodymium or cadmium/selenium (inclusion reds and oranges). Avoid breathing dust.
crocus-martis-sold-by-us-suppliers-nv7ve: Crocus martis sold by US suppliers today is a micronized synthetic red iron oxide (Bayferrox 180) with a bluish-purple tint, not the old calcined iron sulfate. Use it like red iron oxide; recipes written for the old sulfate-bearing kind used more of it, because that kind lost about a fifth of its weight in firing.
not-classified-as-hazardous-lanxess-bayf: Not classified as hazardous (Lanxess Bayferrox 180 M data; red iron oxide pigment). Nuisance dust; older Laguna SDS notes about 4% amorphous silica.
natural-iron-titanium-ore-sold-as-owmfed: Natural iron-titanium ore sold as sand-sized grains (about 30–270 mesh) to give dark brown specks in glazes and clay bodies. This grade is an altered ilmenite, about 64% TiO2 and 29% iron oxide; the grains do not fully dissolve, so the calculated chemistry overstates what goes into the glass.
not-classified-under-ghs-prince-minerals: Not classified under GHS (Prince Minerals ''Granular Ilmenite'' SDS, rev. 2014-10, distributed by Laguna and Axner); contains up to 0.5% quartz.
bentonite-sold-by-carl-ja-ger-lwhw4v: Bentonite sold by Carl Jäger (Germany) and Bodmer Ton (Switzerland), and with the same analysis by Silica Nordic (Denmark): a swelling montmorillonite clay used at 0.5-2% (up to 3%) to keep glazes in suspension and to harden the raw glaze coat. It is much richer in lime (6% CaO) and lower in silica than American sodium bentonite (Volclay), so use this record when a European recipe calls for ''Bentonit''.
bentonite-dust-may-contain-crystalline-s: Bentonite dust may contain crystalline silica (quartz or cristobalite); avoid breathing the dust.
white-low-iron-bentonite-sold-by-kd46hw: White, low-iron bentonite sold by Spanish pottery suppliers (Prodesco, Marphil) as a glaze suspender and plasticiser. The sheet gives it as about 80% montmorillonite and 17% opal-C/cristobalite, which explains the very high silica.
contains-about-17-cristobalite-opal-c-1k: Contains about 17% cristobalite/opal-C according to the supplier; cristobalite is a form of crystalline silica, so avoid breathing the dust.
natural-sodium-bentonite-mined-and-proce: Natural sodium bentonite mined and processed near Miles, Queensland; sold to potters by Northcote Pottery Supplies as ''Bentonite - Trubond'' and used at 1-3% to keep glazes in suspension.
unimin-tds-warns-the-product-contains-k4: Unimin TDS warns the product contains free crystalline silica (quartz). Avoid breathing the dust.
have-a-system-to-your-process-uy0twl: Have a system to your process. Record what you do in a consistent way, and keep the records together. Developing a good system of glazing and mixing will reduce the time, effort, and errors.
mixing-your-glazes-to-a-consistent-kfntn: Mixing your glazes to a consistent density, or specific gravity, will greatly aid you in achieving your goals. Write down the measurement (either density or specific gravity) so you can track the effects of changes.
establish-a-consistent-bisque-firing-sch: Establish a consistent bisque firing schedule, for both cone and rate. This will set a baseline for your wares to have a standard absorption rate of the glazes. Reducing variability in this area of the process will aid in exploring and controlling glazes.
bisque-firing-bisc-firing-bisque-firing-: bisque firing, bisc firing, bisque-firing, prep, methods
never-sweep-the-studio-or-glaze-eti5ut: Never sweep the studio or glaze room. The best way to clean the floor is with a wet mop. A contractor sponge will work well for a spot with a tough layer. Dust is the inevitable result of working with clay and glaze materials, and sweeping stirs it up.
use-permanent-labels-on-glaze-materials-: Use permanent labels on glaze materials and glaze containers. This is doubly important for hazardous materials, common in glaze colorants and thus in glazes. Paper or tape labels tend to come off when wet, and glazes are full of water. It is a simple matter to cross off a marking that no longer applies to a container.
small-amounts-of-epsom-salts-1-q1tjq9: Small amounts of epsom salts, 1 - 2 tablespoons to 20 lbs., will keep glaze particles in suspension and avoid a hardened mass on the bottom of the bucket.
glaze-tiles-can-be-made-with-1u67bt3: Glaze tiles can be made with a 1/4" hole, and then attached to the glaze bucket handle. The glaze tile can be extruded at the correct thickness to mimic your ware, labeled with a batch number pressed into the clay, and banded with your favorite slip(s). Then you can tell at a glance what the effect will be. Repeat for all your common clays to get a spectrum of possibilities at your fingertips.
after-putting-a-cone-in-the-swloel: After putting a cone in the kiln sitter, use masking tape to cover it. The tape will protect the cone from getting knocked off while loading pots, and burns off cleanly in the firing.
